issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For a childhood trauma defined as witnessing domestic violence, 'Body Shame' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type because it implies a direct bodily violation or injury to the patient rather than witnessing violence between others. While witness trauma can lead to guilt, fear, mistrust, or betrayal appraisals, shame specifically about 'what happened to my body' is clinically implausible here unless there is an additional unreported direct trauma.

issues.item: Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
issues.explanation: The memory profile centers on disorganized, overwhelmed recall of a witnessed domestic violence event. 'Auditory Recall' can occur in witness trauma, but in this profile it is the only strongly sensory-perceptual memory item and is not linked to any trigger items or matching contextual content. Given the formulation shows Triggers disconnected from Memory and the rest of the profile emphasizes global threat and appraisal-driven coping, this item stands out as poorly integrated and may reflect a different trauma presentation.

vignette:
Marisol Vega was 26 when she first came to treatment, a single school counselor who had built a life in the same city where she had grown up. Raised in a Latin American family, she spoke with the careful precision of someone who had learned early to read a room before she entered it. Her trauma dated back to childhood, to the years when she witnessed domestic violence in the home. She did not describe a single scene as though it were neatly contained; instead, she spoke of the atmosphere of those years - the sounds from another room, the sudden shifts in adult voices, the sense that danger could arrive without warning and be followed by everyone pretending nothing had happened. What stayed with her most was not only what she saw, but the certainty that the people and systems around her were not going to protect her. As she put it, the people who should have stepped in let her down, and that knowledge has never felt fully in the past.

In the years after, Marisol developed a way of moving through the world that kept her scanning for danger in other people. Even now, she watches faces quickly and carefully, as if checking who might turn unsafe. At home, she is rarely fully settled; she described feeling on guard even inside her own apartment, with a persistent need to know where everyone is and what is behind her. When she sits in a café, a staff room, or a meeting with parents at school, she chooses a chair with her back against the wall so she can see the whole room. If someone comes up behind her or touches her unexpectedly on the shoulder, she reacts with clear alarm before she can compose herself. She knows this can make her seem tense or overly alert, but to her it feels like common sense. In her mind, people cannot be trusted to be harmless simply because they look calm.

Her work as a school counselor has become one of the places where this vigilance is most active. She is good at her job and conscientious with students, but she notices herself tracking certain adults in the building - especially those who seem angry, loud, or unpredictable. She is more guarded in meetings when conflict arises between caregivers, and she remains internally prepared for something to escalate. The school setting also keeps her in daily contact with reminders of childhood. Hallways, offices, and certain apartment complexes near the school can unexpectedly bring the memory back to her with a force that surprises even her. She said there are moments when something in the surroundings - a raised voice through a wall, a particular smell, the look of a doorway - can return the whole memory at once, without warning, and she feels as though she is no longer in the present. When that happens, she has to stop what she is doing until the wave passes.

Trying to explain what happened has always been difficult for Marisol. In intake she would begin speaking clearly, then lose the thread partway through, as if the story became too large to hold in language. When the memory returns, she becomes overwhelmed by emotion and has to stop mid-sentence, sometimes looking down and going quiet for several seconds before she can continue. She described wanting to make sense of it, but finding that the facts slip away under the weight of what she feels. She also ruminates on prevention, revisiting the past in an effort to determine what could have been done differently. She often asks herself whether she acted in ways that made things worse, whether she should have spoken up sooner, been quieter, been more careful, or somehow anticipated what was coming. Although she intellectually knows she was a child, she still returns to the belief that the event happened because of the way she acted.

These thoughts have made ordinary life feel narrower over time. Marisol avoids going to or near the place where the violence happened, even when it requires planning a longer route or turning down invitations that would bring her close to that neighborhood. The avoidance is not dramatic, but it is consistent, and she has organized enough of her schedule around it that it now shapes where she shops, drives, and spends time after work. In her personal life, it has also contributed to a growing distance from people she might otherwise have let closer, because she finds it hard to relax when she cannot fully predict someone's intentions. She presents as thoughtful and articulate, yet there is a visible strain in how carefully she manages her surroundings and her words.

What finally brought Marisol to seek help was the realization that she was no longer able to dismiss these experiences as simply being "careful." The tension at home, the startle when touched, the abrupt flooding of memory, and the effort of keeping herself away from reminders had begun to feel exhausting. She came hoping for some relief from being constantly on guard, but she also admitted to a deeper fear: that if she lets herself stop scanning for danger, something terrible will happen and she will be caught unprepared again. At the same time, what she most hopes for is to understand her own reactions without having to stop in the middle of her story, and to feel safe enough that home, work, and ordinary conversation no longer feel like places where danger might suddenly enter.
